newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Austrian minister tries to smooth bank row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Austrian minister tries to smooth bank row.

text.p: Austrian Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger, seeking to end a coalition row over Bank Austria's privatisation, said on Tuesday that German WestLB 's first option on a majority stake did not preclude a sale within Austria.

"WestLB's first refusal on the AVZ shares expires on March 31, 2001, making it thoroughly possible for AVZ to sell its stake in Austria after that date," said Edlinger, a member of Chancellor Viktor Klima's Social Democrats.

Edlinger was responding to charges from conservative coalition partner the People's Party that the Social Democrats hushed up the deal between Vienna City's holding company AVZ and Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale giving the bank first refusal on its 45.15 percent voting stake in Bank Austria
Vienna City has said it wants AVZ to sell the stake within six years.

AVZ, whose board includes Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa and Vienna's Social Democrat mayor Michael Haeupl, awarded WestLB first option on its stake in 1995 when WestLB bought 10.7 percent of Bank Austria.
News of the agreement, apparently at odds with Vienna city plans to privatise Bank Austria while maintaining a majority Austrian interest, only emerged over the weekend.
"This deal was known to all members of the AVZ board, including the People's Party appointee," Edlinger insisted.

People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel said he knew nothing of the agreement, however. His Economy Minister Hannes Farnleitner went further and demanded the annulment of last January's sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria.
"Either WestLB gives up its right or the sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria must be reversed," Farnleitner told Austrian television during a trip to Spain.
The People's Party only agreed with reluctance to the sale of the nation's most conservative bank to socialist stronghold Bank Austria.
"There can be no question of anulling the sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria," Edlinger said.

The latest privatisation row, which comes six months after the government finally managed to wind up the sale of Creditanstalt following six years of effort, could prove embarrassing for Bank Austria.
It is trying to drum up interest in a three billion schillings ($246.6 million) preference share issue later this year and is organising a complicated share swap with Creditanstalt investors.
The Austrian government also wants to sell its 17 percent Bank Austria stake as soon as possible.

"On paper Bank Austria should not have a problem finding buyers for its preference shares, which are trading at a hefty discount to its ordinaries. But these political arguments are not helpful," an international analyst said.
Bank Austria preferred shares were four schillings up at 425 on low volume of 2,130 lots in early afternoon trade. Its ordinaries were two schillings lower at 770. ($ = 12.16 Austrian Schillings)
